Partitioning of organic matter (OM) is important because POM that escapes grazing, sinks to the deeper waters and represents a part of CO2 that is effectively taken up and stored. DOM is degraded by bacteria releasing CO2 to the atmosphere and is not usually transferred to deeper waters. Recent studies have shown under elevated temperatures phytoplankton produce more DOM and there is an increase in bacterial respiration i.e. the OM is degraded faster and CO2 is released. Both the processes decrease the effective CO2 removal from the atmosphere. My doctoral thesis titled, ""Dynamics of particulate and dissolved organic matter in relation to changing physicochemical conditions in the central and eastern Arabian Sea"" is broadly divided into 3 objectives: i) To study the distribution of DOM and POM during the SW and NE monsoon. 30-day cruises have been conducted in Aug 2017 and Aug 2018, and a 3rd is planned in Dec 2019. The last systematic study that included the eastern AS (west coast of India) was in 1995-96. Hence, the data set produced will be used to look at the changes that have taken place over the two decades, as several studies have pointed out that the northern Indian Ocean is warming faster than other oceans. ii) Assessing the amount of CO2 taken up by phytoplankton in the surface waters during SW and NE monsoon. iii) To study the degradation of OM by bacteria under increased temperatures. Bacteria contribute to degrading about 75% of the annual net phytoplankton production and control CO2 flux from the ocean to the atmosphere. Increased temperatures are known to enhance bacterial activity, yet there are no studies from the AS. During my tenure at East Anglia University I plan to focus on the third objective. Prof Carol Robinson studies the role of marine bacteria, phytoplankton, and zooplankton in global carbon cycle, and how it varies with space, time, and changing environmental conditions. I intend to learn to design the experiments to study the bacterial degradation under increased temperatures. Despite our great dependence on the coasts the studies that look at the degradation of OM are absent. The difference in the OM affects the nature of fisheries with carnivorous and planktivore fishes dominating the northern and southern sector of the west coast of India, respectively. On return, I intend to employ similar experiments to enhance the understanding of OM cycling along our coast

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Investigation into distinct pathways for AMR proliferation in Indian context
descriptions: Summary -|In my doctoral research, I am investigating the acquisition of the ability to defy treatment among pathogens and the spread of this ability through environmental routes.  The particular focus of this research is on the role of customs and constraints that are unique to India. My doctoral placement at James Hutton Institute (JHI) would permit me to analyse the levels of genes that confer the ability to resist treatment (antibiotics) in the varied complex environmental matrices.  Additionally, our current collaborators at JHI have recently broken the ground on analysis and modelling of the relevant data. My placement at JHI would help me learn these statistical tools and make meaningful inferences from our antimicrobial resistance data. |Brief details of PhD project-|Pathogens are increasingly developing resistance to the antimicrobials that were once effective. Antimicrobial resistance is now a global public health threat and is predicted to claim about 10 million lives annually in India by 2050. In my doctoral research, I am mapping the pathways through which antimicrobial resistance spreads in environment within Indian context. Armed with this knowledge, we would be able to protect public health from the threat of pathogens resisting treatment. An important distinction is that the Indian environment is unique in its pollutant loading and human behaviour and so the observations from other environments in past have not permitted designing effective interventions. I am looking for the hotspots of resistance in India and identifying the primary exposure routes. One of the major exposure route to antibiotic resistance genes in our region is ritual mass bathing, wherein millions of pilgrims assemble and bathe together in the Ganga river. For past two years, I have been tracking the elevation of antibiotic resistance genes downstream to major bathing ghats and its correlation with major bathing events. |Purpose of the placement visit -|One of the biggest challenges in this study is that majority of the environmental bacteria are not culturable; the culture based methods barely scratch the surface of environmental reservoir of resistance. Another challenge peculiar to Indian samples, is the excess of sewage, proteins and other inhibitors in samples that thwarts their analysis. As such, a placement with Dr. Lisa Avery at JHI would enable me to troubleshoot the issues in removing the inhibitors, analysing the samples, and learning statistical tools to do microbial source tracking. This is essential for success in mapping the pathways of antimicrobial resistance in India.|

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: DYNAMICS OF ENDOSYMBIONT INTERACTION IN BEMISIA TABACI(GENNADIUS)
descriptions: The project entitled in this placement program is ""Localization of the BEV endosymbiont in the planthopper Cicadella viridis using Fluorescence in-situ hybridization and examining the evidence for the presence of endosymbiont in host plants of Cicadella viridis"" belongs to insect order Hemiptera.|The Hemipteran insects are important vectors of plant disease worldwide. The Mentor group in the UK studies Hemiptera-symbiont interactions in the green planthopper, but the techniques learned are applicable to my Ph.D.research study system where the whitefly Bemisia tabaci, subject of my research is an Hemipteran pest which harbors same endosymbionts reported in planthopper. Bemisia tabaci is one of the devastating insect pests of 20th century, being cosmopolitan and polyphagous.Bemisia tabaci is an important vector of viral and bacterial disease to plants, and is a source of considerable economic loss.Bemisia tabaci known to attack mor than 700 species of plants and recorded to vector more than 100 plant viruses. Importantly, the competence of insects for transmitting disease is partly determined by their microbial symbionts. The presence bacterial endosymbionts(Proteobacteria) like Portiera, Rickettsia, Wolbacchia Hamiltonella in B.tabaci influence their biology, reproductive physiology and their interaction with other organisms or the environment and mainly have a role in plant virus transmission.My PhD research objectives deals with the spatial and temporal variation of endosymbionts in whiteflies of different agroclimatic zones, effect of endosymbionts on biology of whitefly and their intraction studies.The research gap in the path way of our research work and part of third objective needs further exploration of endosymbionts entry into whiteflies and there is no much-confirmed findings related to the transmission of perticular endosymbionts between insects species. There is no confirmed findings related to the transmissin and inheritance of endosymbionts through the host plants which the whiteflies feed. So the perticular training will try to reveal Hostplant-endosymbiont-insect interaction and their transmissin pathway within the environment. The endosymbints under study have potential role in combating Hemipteran pests and the viral disease they spread so the proposed study is basic to reveal their interactions to open up the use of same endosymbionts in management of hemiptran pests specially whiteflies and its transmitted diseases.|The work would establish a new partnership for better understanding insect vectors of plant diseases, with the capacity for novel innovation that would then reduce plant disease burden and aid sustainable agriculture and improve economic development.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Influence of Obstacles on Large Scale Flows: Climatic Aspects
descriptions: Orography and the surface contrast between land and ocean (including temperature, surface energy balance and roughness) over South Asia act as an important driver of the South Asian monsoon which greatly influences the energy, food and water security of South Asian countries. Although only a relatively small fractional change in monsoon precipitation occurs from year to year, it has a major effect on the health and prosperity of more than one billion people residing in the region. The energy generated from hydropower, covering almost 25% of the electricity demand of the South Asian countries, is reliant on the rain water. The GDP of countries like India, which are strongly dependent on agriculture (15%), is affected due to crop failure because of excess or deficit rainfall. Excess rainfall also introduces substantial flood risk, which can drown victims and damage buildings leaving people homeless, as in the case of 2014 floods over Pakistan, India and China where nearly 300 people died and many were left homeless. Therefore, accurate prediction of monsoon and its future becomes essential. Several theories have been proposed to explain the origin, process, strength, variability and distribution of monsoon, but understanding and predictive skill are still developing. Simulation of the monsoon flow using climate models has been notoriously difficult, with large biases developing with lead time. For example, it was projected by Bhaskaran et al. (1995) that a significant increase in precipitation would occur due to a rise in CO2 concentration over recent decades, but no such trend has been detected, questioning the robustness of such projections.  One of the key reasons behind model uncertainty is the lack of proper orographic representation in the climate models (Anand et al. 2018). My PhD thesis therefore aims at addressing these issues by understanding the role of these large scale obstacles on atmospheric flows using a hierarchy of models to bridge the gap between theory and realistic global circulation models.|Through the proposed placement at the University of Reading we aim to develop the scientific underpinning for the influence of large-scale orography on the flow across South Asia, beginning with idealised theoretical frameworks and models using simplified configurations as a stepping stone towards more comprehensive models with realistic topography. We will try to address a part of my PhD research problem by understanding the role of orography in driving monsoonal circulation and the impact on climatological variables through a simple water-covered planet (aquaplanet), in which we will introduce different orographic components in stages. This will improve our understanding of the large scale monsoonal circulation and help to formulate the theoretical expressions for drag associated with the Rossby waves which, although they are explicitly resolved in climate models, have an uncertain functional dependence on orographic parameters. |

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: A Study of convection over Bay of Bengal using cloud-resolving Large Eddy Simulation
descriptions: Clouds play an important role in the energy budget and water cycle of the climate system. Given their importance in the climate system, an accurate representation of clouds in large-scale numerical models is of paramount importance. However, given the limited observations available, a lot remain to be understood about clouds and their representation in numerical models. Moist convection in the atmosphere (manifested in the form of clouds) vertically transports heat and moisture. In the Indian context, the Bay of Bengal (BoB) provides an excellent natural laboratory to understand atmospheric convection, because many convective systems keep forming and dissipating over its warm waters. Convective transfer of moisture and heat in the form of turbulent fluxes over BoB is not explored much and is not resolved in Global and Regional climate models due to coarser resolutions. Thus, the present study is an attempt to augment the current state of understanding of convection phenomenon over BoB using a high-resolution cloud resolving Large Eddy Simulation (LES) model. The study will focus on understanding the relationship between sea surface temperature (SST) and moist convection over BoB. The coupled atmosphere-ocean dynamics related to formation of convection over BoB will be investigated by using ocean mixed layer model instead of prescribed SST. In addition, the role of model resolution and different microphysics assumptions on atmospheric convection will be investigated. Knowledge gained from this study will be very useful for the development of convection parameterization schemes used in global and regional models for producing more accurate simulations both for the short term predictions and long-term climate change projections.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Metal-organic framework (MOF) modified functional materials for electrochemical water splitting and fuel cell application
descriptions: Summary of the scientific background and importance of the research area:||Solar energy has come up as one of the most promising alternative sources of energy. Technological advancements have made it possible to convert solar energy into electrical energy; which in turn can be used for our practical purposes. But, there are still some obstacles to be overcome, so as to make the large scale use of solar energy, feasible. These are: |(1) Efficient storage of this energy in the form of fuel molecules for later use (minimum loss of energy in the pathway). |(2) Obtaining high energy density while combusting these fuel molecules.|(3) Improving the performance of the solar panels in converting solar energy to electrical energy.  ||Our research goal is to address these issues and come up with probable solutions. My PhD research at the home institute is to work on the first two points mentioned above. Hydrogen is one of the highest energy density fuel molecules, having the potential to be used for high energy demanding works (e.g. industrial use). Our research is to be able to use water and sunlight as the source of obtaining this supply of hydrogen.||Research work of PhD project:| |Researchers around the world have developed several materials that have the capability to generate H2 from water using sunlight/ electricity. But, most of them cannot fulfill the benchmarks of efficiency, stability, and cost-effectiveness at the same time, so as to make these materials commercially feasible. So, our research goal is to develop a relatively low-cost material with high stability and efficiency, to perform the process of generation of hydrogen from water. For this work, we prepare hybrid materials out of metal complexes and metal-organic frameworks (MOFs)[porous materials] and study their catalytic activity towards electrochemical splitting of water molecules.||Proposed research work of Placement project:||The purpose of this placement project is to address the third point of the list. The solar cells used commercially are all silicon-based and, enhancing the efficiency of these kinds of solar cells increases its cost to a huge extent. Perovskite is a relatively new material that holds the potential to be used in developing more efficient solar cells; and most importantly, these would be much more cost-effective. But, these materials are less stable in the presence of moisture; which makes its use difficult for practical purposes. So, our research goal in this placement project is to develop a range of hybrid materials out of perovskite and metal-organic frameworks (MOFs)[porous materials], in order to enhance the stability and performance of these materials. In the course of this process, we plan to synthesize and fully characterize these hybrid materials. Then we shall study the functional properties of these materials employing the sophisticated techniques available in the host institute.|

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Optimization of anaerobic digestion for removal of antibiotic resistant genes from dairy and|poultry sector
descriptions: Antimicrobial resistance threatens the onset of a global post-antibiotic era wherein our stronghold against infectious diseases, the antibiotics are no longer effective. WHO has estimated a loss of 10 million lives by the year 2050 due to drug-resistant infections. The major driver of antimicrobial resistance is environmental contamination with antibiotics and other co-selectors. The dairy and poultry industries in India are one of the largest in the world and are a key consumer and releaser of antibiotics into the environment. However, little is known about the environmental fate of these antibiotics and their impact on antimicrobial resistance.||My doctoral research asks four major questions: a. What is the contribution of the Indian dairy and poultry industry to the antimicrobial resistance and pharmaceutical load in the environment? b. Which farm practices are best at preventing the proliferation of antimicrobial resistance? c. What is the best way to compost the waste of dairy and poultry industry for minimizing the risk of transmitting resistance through agriculture and food? and d. What is the relationship between the antimicrobial levels and antimicrobial resistance in the receiving environment?||For my doctoral research at IIT-Roorkee, I am profiling and mapping the antimicrobial resistance in the Indian dairy and poultry industry on a national level to answer the first three major research questions. To establish the relationship between the known drivers of resistance, such as pharmaceuticals, it is necessary to quantify the co-selectors of antimicrobial resistance in diverse samples.||My placement at the University of Nottingham will provide the expertise necessary to analyze the different co-selectors of antimicrobial resistance viz., antibiotics and their conjugates, insecticides, pesticides from a variety of samples which include soil, wastewater, dung, manure, litter, droppings. In-depth training in analytical techniques and method development is the major objective of this Ph.D. placement.||With the detection and quantification of co-selectors, it would be easier to identify the factors responsible for the selection of resistance and map their impact. In order to regulate the dairy industry, the national level profiling of the situation of antimicrobial resistance needs to be correlated with the co-selectors, for which my placement at the University of Nottingham is essential.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Understanding of the Primary Process Responsible for the Non-targeted Genotoxic Effect Induced by Fungicides Using Femtosecond Stimulated Raman Spectr
descriptions: Fungi are the most significant pathogenic organism which causes the greatest amount of damage to plants and crops worldwide. Development of fungicides has significantly decreased the effect of fungi on crops and plants by their targeted action. However, the fungicides have non-targeted effect also on the humans as well as other organisms, which lead to several serious diseases such as disruptions of endocrine balance in organism resulting in nausea, cancer, fetus malformations, movement dysfunction and behavioral changes.  Indeed, it has been shown that the exposure of fungicides depict the genotoxic and cytotoxic effect on its consumers. Hence, understanding of the mechanism of the non-targeted action of fungicides causing these genotoxic and cytotoxic effects is important to design effective fungicides with less non-targeted effects. |Recently, we have studied the mechanism of genotoxicity of fungicides using spectroscopic and molecular dynamics simulation studies.1 It has been found that the fungicide dodine damages the DNA duplex by removing the water from its adenine-thymine region in the minor groove which causes to the broadening of the groove width along with elongation of its DNA strand. Moreover, we have also found that the fungicide disrupt the structure of myoglobin at very less concentration by hydrophobic effect.2 These studies were performed mostly using the steady state spectroscopic technique, hence, the information about the dynamics of fungicides causing the structural change of DNA, protein  leading to genotoxicity is not yet known. |Femtosecond stimulated Raman spectroscopy (FSRS) is a versatile ultrafast spectroscopic technique that provides vibrational structural information with high temporal (50 fs) and spectral (10 cmâˆ’1) resolution in the ground and excited state.3-4 Hence, we propose to understand the structural change of protein and DNA by fungicides carbendazim (and its derivatives) using FSRS technique. We will use the FSRS technique to understand the role of the hydrogen bond of water and fungicide in the structural change of protein and DNA. We will also probe the carbonyl of protein and phosphate of DNA to understand the primary process involved in their structural change. The detailed understanding of fungicide induced DNA and protein damage may guide for the development of new fungicides with minimal non-targeted action.     |1. Sarkar, S.; Singh, P. C., Mechanistic Aspects of Fungicide Induced DNA Damage: Spectroscopic and Molecular Dynamics Simulation Studies. J. Phys. Chem. B 2019.|2. Biswas, B.; Singh, P. C., Does Fungicide ""Dodine"" Unfold Protein like Kosmo-Chaotropic Agent? J. Phys. Chem. B 2019.|3. Hall, C. R.; Conyard, J.; Heisler, I. A.; Jones, G.; Frost, J.; Browne, W. R.; Feringa, B. L.; Meech, S. R., Ultrafast Dynamics in Light-Driven Molecular Rotary Motors Probed by Femtosecond Stimulated Raman Spectroscopy. J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2017, 139 (21), 7408-7414.||

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Development of Innovative Waste Utilization Methodologies for Material Removal Processes
descriptions: Sustainable development saves environment, economy and full fills human need of natural resources. Sustainable processes and technologies conserve natural resources for future generation. In this domain, our target is to maintain the sustainability in manufacturing sector by utilizing the machining waste in different routes.|Manufacturing industries worldwide, face problems in tackling machining scrap, which is produced via different machining operations (e.g. drilling, grinding and cutting, etc.). Present studies focus on developing different techniques to address machining scrap problems. We have invented new approaches in this domain, and use machining waste in an economic way by developing new materials in the form of micrometre-sized powder, coating and 3D printing. Direct utilization of machining waste/scrap during the manufacturing operation is a challenging task, which we have done successfully using new processes and technologies. The proposed research work put forward the best solution to minimize machining waste as well as reduce the environmental impact. The techniques can be used for the production of various coating and 3D-part printing (additive manufacturing) with machining waste. The developed technologies can be used for a broad range of engineering applications, such as repairing, decoration, and, patterns etc. |My research work is going on under the supervision of Prof. Harpreet Singh (IIT Ropar, India) and Prof. Christopher Berndt (Swinburne University of Technology, Australia), and our purpose is to commercialize these technologies. In the next few months, we plan to optimize the process parameters. Waste is the biggest problems all over the world and hence we are focusing on solving problems related to scrap/waste with an innovative concept. |Finally, we need to implement these new processes in manufacturing industries globally, which will play an important role in saving the environment as well as in production of a new class of product from the machining waste. Therefore, further development of proposed technologies into worldwide industrial applications is required, and needs more attention and investigation. Newton-Bhabha Fund Ph.D. Placement Programme will play a crucial role in shaping my research career. The purpose of my placement visit is to explore the proposed sustainable technologies and enhance my research by working with host specialists to build networks. Moreover, I will gain valuable national and international exposure and experience in the management of global research projects. This programme will also help to access facilities and skills training from two research-intensive universities. |

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Planning for Water, Energy and Food Nexus for sustainable development of Bundelkhand region of Uttar Pradesh State
descriptions: The world is facing an immense amount of the pressure of urbanization, economic growth, technological advancement, climate change, population growth, international trade, economic growth, expanding the discourse on security (Albrecht, 2018) and globalization. To maintain sustainable growth, the primary challenge is to manage the demand and supply of available resources and to ensure the security of water, energy, and food (WEF). These three resources have a complex interaction among each other. To minimize risk and maximize human-environment security, optimization of WEF connections is required. The demands for WEF are estimated to increase by 40 %, 50 %, and 35% respectively by the year 2030 (USNIC, 2012). Explicit interaction needs to be established between these three sectors to find optimal solution for WEF security, which is need of the hour. |Frequent drought in Bundelkhand has not only made the region water-scarce but also poverty-stricken. This has led to mass outmigration, farmer suicides, starvation, deaths, and the decline in agriculture production, drinking water shortage and indebtedness. It has a huge social, economic, and environmental impact. The accentuated water stress situation, people are stuck in a vicious cycle of low income, low output, and negligible saving, which in turn affects the cycle of food and energy. In this region, 76. 3% of people still rely on Kerosene as the main source of energy for lighting and 64.4% of the population use fuelwood for cooking, in spite of having huge potential for hydro and solar energy. Major challenges and gaps are identified in terms of water, food, and energy by using a systematic methodology to identify the multiple interactions among the subsystems. After identification of the parameters, that control the development of this area especially in terms of water, food, and energy of Bundelkhand region, the recommendations will be made based on the findings. |The research topic opens new vistas to develop an innovative strategy for socio-economic development in the field of planning to find a sustainable approach at the grassroots level. Newton Bhabha Fellowship provides an integrated approach to look forward solutions but also gives me international exposure to learning from brilliant minds globally. It gives me creative freedom that I enjoy by interacting with various stakeholders from different disciplines. Professionally, it will increase my knowledge and exposure to a holistic and interdisciplinary approach to find an innovative solution. The research is in-line with the objectives and so it will help me a great deal to find an optimal solution. Co-creation will help me develop my research at different stages. WEF security being the biggest challenge of today's world, it's very important to work together on such project. Personally, I will get chance to interact with scholars of the UK, a very different culture from India and I am very interested in knowing their traditions.|

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Effect of traditional rice beer (Apong) on the gut bacterial profile of Mishing ethnic community of Assam|
descriptions: The human intestinal tract is colonised by various friendly microorganisms, which are collectively called as gut microbiota. Such microorganisms helps the host in digestion of food, secretes essential vitamins, regulates the immune system among others benefits. However, the members of the gut microbiota varies among population. Such a change is determined by age, sex, life-style and diet of an individual, in which diet and life-style plays an important role. The aim of my PhD thesis is to profile the gut microbiota of the Mishing community (an ethnic community of India with simple lifestyle and traditional diet). As a part of my doctoral study, I wish to identify the bacterial community residing the gut of mishing community and the role those microbes are playing in keeping the host healthy. Moreover, the focus is also to understand how disruption in the bacterial community effects the host and how the normal condition can be restored. |Through the proposed placement, I wish to carry out the computational analysis component of the PhD. Through this approach we can understand the specific interactions of microbe with the host cells. |

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Effect of ligands, dispersion medium and analyte properties on the stability of gold nanoparticles for optical detection application
descriptions: Implantable biomaterials in the form of joint replacements, orthopaedic implants and cardiovascular stents have gained popularity for elevating lifestyle of the aging population and addressing unique medical complications. They are generally made up of alloys comprising nickel, cobalt, chromium, titanium and iron. Though they are chemically inert and biocompatible, hostile microenvironment and heavy mechanical action lead to their degradation. As a result metal ions are released into the body and accumulate in the tissues. Though the body tolerates and utilises the metal ions to a certain level, excess concentration lead to metal toxicity and adverse health effects. Co, Cr and Ni confer the highest toxicity. Though medical exposure to such implants delivers the highest systemic metal ion concentrations, environmental exposure through contaminated food and water also has a major role in Co and Ni toxicity. In developing countries like India, people are still at risk of consuming contaminated water due to inefficient monitoring and poor filtration techniques. Even though various analytical techniques are available for their detection, they are expensive and require scientific expertise. Therefore there is a requirement of a simple low cost method for metal detection in biological and water samples to provide portable point-of-care testing of metal ions. Current progress in nanotechnology provides ample opportunities for precise designing of biosensors with high sensitivity and specificity. Nanoparticles possess unique properties in terms of high surface to volume ratio, biocompatibility, ease of surface modification and surface plasmon resonance making them ideal for sensing and diagnostics.|The aim of this study is to develop a colorimetric assay for detection of Co and Ni in body fluids and/or water samples using modified gold nanoparticles (GNPs). Many studies available in literature have shown colorimetric and rapid detection of heavy metals like As, Hg, Cu, Cr, Pb, Ca and Ba in aqueous medium using GNPs. Taking lead from that, we aim to study the interaction of Co and Ni ions with simple biomolecular ligands and develop GNPs with surface functionalisation using suitable ligands for selective detection of the metals. The modified gold nanoparticles will be optimised in terms of their surface chemistry, colloidal stability, selectivity and sensitivity of detection using various characterization techniques. Development of a simple low cost assay for Co and Ni metals in blood serum will help in monitoring the implant integrity and rapid detection of metal toxicity due to its degeneration. This will help in early diagnosis and prevention of life threatening complications. The same assay will provide an on-site testing method for contaminated water and prevent its further circulation and accumulation in the food chain. Thus the proposed work will serve the dual purpose of detecting and monitoring Co and Ni ions in physiological and  water samples.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Fabrication of Optical and Electrochemical Sensors for Biomarkers
descriptions: Development of Biosensors||Our group develops sensors for a wide range of molecules such as biomolecules, food additives, pharmaceuticals etc. These analytes are detected and monitored in samples through electrochemical and fluorescence techniques. For efficient sensing the receptor part of a sensor is chemically modified through nanomaterials, polymers, quantum dots etc. The nanomaterials are generally used for signal amplification in the electrochemical sensing. Whereas in fluorescence sensing, fluorescent nanomaterials are stabilized with biomaterials by adding proteins and other biomolecules to make them biocompatible. |When the receptor part of the sensor is a biomaterial instead of a chemical compound it can specifically interact with the analyte even in the presence of structurally similar and coexisting species. The PhD project is mainly about the modification of the receptor part of the sensor with biological materials such as DNA probes, antigen/antibody, proteins etc. along with the use of nanotechnologies in the development of biosensor. |In this regard, the placement is of significance. In biosensors, the processes for the modification of a receptor part is of utmost care mostly close to physiological conditions. It usually consists of a series of steps employing a lot of technologies. The analytical signal of the receptor shows its physicochemical properties and it can be detected by any methods of detection. Developing new sensors and improving older types of sensors are equally important. New technology provides more sensitive instruments that are quick with better selectivity and sensitivity.|The placement provides a chance to develop a biosensor for the detection of proteins/ antibiotics, where particles are released in the presence of the analyte allowing them to be counted with resistive pulse sensing (RPS). In this technique, a nanoparticle or analyte is passed through a nanoscale channel causing a change in conductance of the channel. This creates a resistive pulse which is related to the physical properties of the analyte. The placement also encompasses the study of biomaterials modified with nanomaterials and its use in quantification of proteins. |

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Synthesis of novel heterocyclic molecules and their biological applications
descriptions: Over a period of 7 years, my PhD goal is to capture a broader and more detailed picture of malaria incidence in different parts of the world, and to identify questions and study sites that will help national and international programs understand and control malaria more efficiently, with the long term goal of global malaria eradication. The structure-based design of new bioactive molecules involves, as a crucial step, the development of a reaction strategy which can access a wide chemical diversity and structural variety of potentially bioactive products. Achieving the goal of malaria elimination will depend on targeting Plasmodium pathways essential across all life stages. Rapidly increasing resistance to practically all currently used drugs has drawn attention for search for more potential, highly-effective, long-lasting vaccine antimalarials with novel mechanism of action, targeting multiple stages of the Plasmodium falciparum life cycle, is likely to be important for the abolition of this pathogen. Ideally antimalarial agents that exhibit multi-stage activities against drug-resistant strains of malaria parasites represent good starting points for beginning of next generation antimalarial therapies, thus impacting prevention, treatment and transmission of disease. To facilitate the progression of such agents into the development phase, we have been working to develop hydroxyethylamine molecules that can target on different sexual & asexual life cycle stages of P. falciparum. Hydroxyethylamine derivatives offers the hope of a new series for the treatment, prevention and, ultimately, eradication of malaria. Oral administration of hydroxyethylamine in mouse models result in effective clearance of liver and blood sexual, asexual stages as well as effective inhibition when combined with CQ, antimalarial drug.The combined presence of hydroxyethylamine and cyclic amines was observed as crucial for the activity. |Moreover Prof. Edward Anderson's research encompasses all aspects of synthetic organic chemistry, with a particular focus on the total synthesis of biologically active molecules, and the development of new reactions including cascade processes. This placement will not only develop my experimental skills and knowledge across a broad range of organic chemistry (due to the expansive nature of research themes in Prof Anderson's group and this Department as a whole), but will also open up possibilities for future collaboration between Prof Anderson and my PhD advisor, Prof Ramesh Chandra.  I will bring my knowledge of medicinal chemistry from my PhD to bear on natural products with anti-leishmanial activity, with the aim of developing new antiparasitic natural product derivatives. It will be possible to exchange materials for testing against P. falciparum from the Anderson group, which would establish a new line of joint research between the two groups, with an expanded library of compounds for anti-parasitic evaluation in both our Universities.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Revisiting Indian Cercosporae Using Sequence and Classical Based Approaches
descriptions: Pulses, are edible seeds of leguminous crops and are a staple food source for the majority of India's population of 1.3 billion. Pulses are a main source of non-meat protein for approximately 1/3rd of the Indian population, with demand growing due to the expanding Indian population. Mungbean, locally known as greengram is one the most important pulse crops grown and consumed in India. It currently ranks third among all pulses grown within India after chickpeas and pigeonpeas. It is a versatile crop that only takes 60-65 days to harvest. It has a high protein content (23%), is also rich in dietary fibre, B vitamins, and minerals, particularly iron, potassium, magnesium and zinc, and is naturally low in fat. Iron deficiency has remained a top cause of disability in India for the past decade. Pulses like mungbean offer significant low-cost nutritional and health benefits that improve diets of the poor and as well as the vegetarian populations of India and other countries across Asia. |However, demand for mungbean in India significantly exceeds current Indian production levels as Indian farmers generally see less than half of the mungbean yield potential, which is often due to the diseases like Cercospora leaf spot (CLS) which is widespread in India. It is caused by Cercospora canescens Ellis and Martin and is a very serious disease of mungbean in South East Asian countries. Upto 60% yield losses have reported due to this disease, yet it is still not widely studied despite it being a major constraint on yield. Many aspects of C. canescens infection biology still need to be investigated before strategies can be developed to improve varieties for resistance and mitigate the disease spread. I am currently studying different Cercospora species which infect a wide range of crops. In this placement I will focus on C. canescens which is a species targeting an economically and nutritionally important crop. With the help of expertise at Rothamsted Research, I will investigate the role of special molecules produced by the fungus called effectors which help in establishing infection in the plants. This will help us understand the disease mechanism better and we can then engineer broad spectrum and possibly durable resistance into new varieties. I will also aim to identify fungal genes responsible for production of a toxin called as cercosporin which is also important for disease establishment and tissue death in infected plants. This will help in developing best disease management strategies and help breeders and scientists develop better Cercospora resistant varieties. The placement will help me learn new tools and techniques especially in fields of bioinformatics and molecular biology which would otherwise not be possible at my home institution. I could then apply these learnings to whole range of other Cercospora species which I am currently studying under my Ph.D. project.||

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: CARDIAC REMODELLING: THE ROLE OF INOSITOL 1,4,5-TRIPHOSPHATE RECEPTORS (InsP3Rs)
descriptions: Along with the overall economic growth and urbanization worldwide, a major fraction of global population has moved towards an unhealthy lifestyle causing a rapid transition in disease over a period of time. Also, large sized population in India has made access to affordable health care at a far reach. Out of all non-communicable diseases (NCDs), cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) account for about half of all the deaths globally, therefore, encouraging intense research and cheaper solution.|The heart undergoes an array of molecular alteration to adapt the increased workload for enhancing the heart functioning which results in the hypertrophied heart (enlarged) followed by Heart Failure (HF), generally termed as cardiac remodelling.  The study of developmental remodelling of heart from neonatal to adult stages has been well established. Also, researchers further observed an overlap between hypertrophic and developmental remodelling and the chief contributor is the recurrence of fetal gene program where calcium (Ca2+) is an important secondary messenger directing these changes. |Global (cytoplasmic) Ca2+ changes in normal cardiac cells (cardiomyocytes) controls the normal beat-to-beat contraction of heart, while the rise in nuclear Ca2+ is studied to trigger cardiac disorder. A myriad of Ca2+ handling proteins plays a role in cardiac pathophysiology by regulating the Ca2+ signals. Among these, we previously have shown the elevated expression of Inositol 1,4,5- triphosphate receptor type-II (InsP3R2) during cardiac hypertrophy. InsP3R2 are predominantly localized on the nuclear envelope and contributes to the increased nuclear Ca2+. This increased nuclear Ca2+ induces re-expression of fetal genes during the development of hypertrophy and HF. Besides this, re-expression of fetal isoforms of many genes during cardiac hypertrophy is basically governed by alternative splicing but the mechanism of its regulation has not been clearly studied. We speculate that, the increased nuclear Ca2+ through InsP3R might be involved in fetal alternative splicing. Therefore, understanding the underlying regulatory mechanism can help to reach a potent therapeutic target for HF.||Through Indo-UK Newton-Bhabha Fund Ph.D. Placement, I will focus on determining the role of InsP3R mediated nuclear Ca2+ on alternative fetal RNA splicing and the underlying molecular mechanisms during cardiac remodelling. My expertise would be extended to explore the role of InsP3R mediated nuclear Ca2+ on alternative splicing pattern of Muscle Lim Protein (MLP) and FHL2 and other sarcomeric proteins which are of prime focus in Dr. Ehler's laboratory such as FHOD3 and EH-myomesin (Iskratsch et al., 2010; Lange et al., 2019). It would also include their differential expression and functional regulation mediated by InsP3R nuclear Ca2+ during cardiac hypertrophy. This will establish a link between two domains of CVDs research and will also extend as collaboration between the two laboratories. |

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: ASSESSMENT OF POLLUTION STATUS AND IS IMPACT ON SOME BIOLOGICAL PARAMETERS OF FISHES INHABITING WATER BODIES OF KATHUA (JAMMU AND KASHMIR, INDIA)
descriptions: Worldwide aquatic ecosystems are under threat. My PhD project involves characterizing and quantifying the impacts of manmade effects such as pollution and global climate change such as warming temperatures on aquatic animals in the Himalayan region. Maintaining food security against the backdrop of population growth is an ongoing challenge in India and South Asia. Whilst intensive brackish water shrimp aquaculture is recognized as a success in terms of improving livelihoods and food production, it is also accompanied by significant risk for farmers due to the heavy economic investment needed and the likelihood of disease and/or pond failure, with climate change accelerating these effects. Shrimp aquaculture is also often accompanied by widespread ecological damage due to mangrove deforestation, use of industrial fishmeal, and pollution caused by pond discharges. Therefore, there is an urgent need to identify new sources of protein for production in these areas that are social-economically and ecologically sustainable and are also resilient to climate change and disease. In India,  culture of small indigenous freshwater fish species crab aquaculture and, e.g. of the mud crab Scylla serrata, can be a sustainable alternative to shrimp as it typically involves the production of a higher value product, requiring less input in terms of economics and biological resources. However, S. serrata is a marine/brackish water species, which geographically limits the use of this resource. Another species with potential as a sustainable commodity species is the freshwater crab Barytelphusacunicularis which is widely distributed throughout India’s vast riverine network, including in the Himalayan region. It is currently hand-picked from the wild for subsistence consumption and/or sale at market and in the restaurant trade and has great, but as of yet untested, potential for culture as it is a continuous breeder with direct development and is highly nutritious. Preliminary studies have confirmed this species is suitable for small scale sustainable aquaculture at low and mid altitudes. However we now wish to test the suitability of this species for aquaculture at high altitudes, including under conditions predicted for future global climate change. This project will enable me to apply my knowledge of Himalayan aquatic ecosystems to a new question, that of testing the suitability for aquaculture of alternative novel species. It will enable me to gain new skills in protocols for measuring the health (physiology) of these animals under these conditions.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Sodium metal oxide cathode materials for secondary sodium-ion and potassium-ion batteries.
descriptions: Energy is a global challenge. It calls for the development of eco-friendly and efficient energy generation along with storage and (mobile) delivery of intermittent renewable energy resources (wind, solar and hydropower). Here, batteries play a key role by storing energy in the form of chemical potentials. This technology led to widespread applications of innovative portable devices and (hybrid) electric vehicles. It has a significant impact on global energy consumption. By 2030, global energy demand is estimated to be 2600 gigawatts per-hour. To meet this global challenge, there is a surge to develop efficient batteries, where cathode forms a crucial component accounting for over 45% of the net cost.|My thesis deals with the development of cathode materials for energy storage as well as mechanistic details associated with structural transformation during the electrochemical reaction. The first reported materials for Li-ion and Na-ion batteries were layered LiCoO2 and NaxCoO2 respectively. The LiCoO2 based Li-ion batteries have unanimously conquered the portable market. However, the scarcity of Li and Co resource has led a question: Is Lithium the new gold? Here, manganese-based Na-ion battery technology can work wonder as a suitable alternative. The Mn-based layered cathode materials are interesting due to the elemental abundance, non-toxicity, elemental economy and occurrence of polymorphism (due to multiple oxidation states Mn+4 to Mn+2). Accurate tuning of the oxidation states can result in a high energy density cathode. In this perspective, Na2Mn3O7 was explored as a cathode for Li-, Na-, K- and Zn-ion batteries (K. Sada et al., ACS Applied Energy Material, 1(10), 5410-5416, 2018; K. Sada et al., ACS Applied Energy Material, 1(12), 6719-6724, 2018 and K. Sada et al., MRS advance, In press). The electrochemical properties of Na2Mn3O7 upon the intercalation of Li, Na, K and Zn delivered reversible capacity of 160, 140, 152, 245 mA h g-1 respectively. Further, the versatile nature of Na2Mn3O7 cathode was investigated from structural point of view. Na2Mn3O7 was examined by dissolving in different salts such as Li2SO4, K2SO4 and ZnSO4. Interestingly, in each case, it resulted in a new polymorph with no matching with standard patterns in materials database.|In continuation, I would like to utilize this opportunity to perform operando/in-situ experiments to understand the insights of the intercalation mechanism as well as polymorphism associated with A2M3O7 (A= Li, Na, K, Zn; M= Mn, V, Ti) class of materials. Moreover, the magnetic properties of materials after charge/discharge redox process will be probed under the guidance of the host (Prof. Sian E Dutton) who is an expert in this field.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Genome-Wide Association Studies for phosphorus use efficiency in diverse bread wheat germplasm|
descriptions: Phosphorus (P) is an essential macronutrient required for growth and development of plants. P is limiting for crop yield on >30% of the world's arable land and, by some estimates, world resources of inexpensive P may be depleted by 2050. As far as India is concerned, most of the Indian soils are either low (49.3% of soils) or medium (48.8% of soils) in available P. India is the biggest importer of phosphatic fertilizers with a 90% dependency. |In India, wheat ranks second in both area (30.7 Mha) and production (99.87 Mt) with an average productivity of 3.368 Mt. To achieve this production, about 20.9% or 1275 Kilotonne of phosphatic fertilizer is consumed by wheat, after rice (27.6%) (www.fertilizer.org). Fertiliser subsidy is the second largest that the Government of India provides after food subsidy. According to the demand for diammonium phosphate (DAP) and single super phosphate (SSP), during the year 2011-2012, and considering P-use efficiency of crops as 10%, the monetary loss of P2O5 was calculated to the tune of INR 7.81 billion. This is a huge loss for the resource poor agricultural sector in India. The major problem with P nutrition is not the soil P content but its bioavailability to the plants. A further incentive to breed P-efficient crops is the fact that the inefficient P fertilizer use is a major cause of environmental pollution through the eutrophication of water bodies. So, to develop crop varieties which can grow and yield, even in poor soil is important. |My research work is to find genomic regions on wheat crop, which governs P use efficiency. I am using Genome Wide Association Approach (GWAS) for finding genomic regions. For this study, both genotypic and phenotypic data are needed. Presently, I have been engaged in conducting phenotyping of ~350 wheat genotypes in both soil and hydroponics system. The root traits in the seedling stage will be scored in hydroponics while other traits related to P use efficiency will be studied in pot culture using soil with low available P and sufficient P until maturity. The phenotypic data will be associated with the genotypic data to find the genomic regions/genes using bioinformatics tools. This will lead to the identification of single nucleotide polymorphic (SNPs) markers associated with the genes/QTLs. Further, the validation of identified genomic regions/genes will be carried out by using Kompetitive Allele Specific PCR (KASP) primer assay using the DNA extracted from a population. The output of my work will be the identification of SNPs and genes can be used for marker-assisted breeding to develop low P tolerant wheat cultivars.| During my placement at NIAB, I will learn the advanced bioinformatics tools related to GWAS, designing KASP primers, KASP assay for validation of identified genomic regions/genes and drafting manuscript.|

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Doped and Undoped 2D Metal Chalcogenide Nanocrystals for Light Harvesting
descriptions: Global fuel consumption is steadily increasing at a rate at which fossil fuel cannot be produced indefinitely, and combusting crude oil is causing irreversible environmental damage. Investigations into sustainable alternatives have identified hydrogen (H2) as a promising energy vector, which can be used directly in an emission-free fuel cell. At the same time, more than 8 million tons of plastic wastes enter the oceans every year, and marine plastic pollution is predicted to outweigh the fish by 2050. Although recycling is increasing, a large fraction of plastic waste cannot be recovered economically, as it is contaminated or mixed with other waste. Photoreforming is a novel approach that enables the conversion of unsorted waste plastic into clean H2 fuel. This process operates at ambient conditions in water and only requires sunlight and a photocatalyst to generate value from waste.|My PhD project at the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science (IACS) is focused on developing advanced semiconducting nanomaterials for H2 generation. Photocatalytic activity depends on various factors such as light absorption, charge separation and surface accessibility. To improve charge separation, we have designed a quasi type-II heterojunction of 1D CdS nanorods covered with CdSe nanoparticles, in which the oxidation and reduction half-reactions are spatially separated. In order to increase the accessibility of both semiconductors, the surface of CdS is not fully covered by CdSe and hence both hole and electron rich centres are exposed and can facility redox reactions. We found that these CdSe-loaded CdS nanorods are 44 times more active than bare CdS nanorods and 22 times more than CdSe nanoparticles. We are now working on the photocatalysis of the hybrid materials based on 2D CdSe and different doped 2D materials with improved photophysical properties. IACS has leading expertise in the synthesis and characterisation of inorganic nanomaterials, but a modern facility for photocatalytic performance testing is not available.|At my host institute Swansea University, I will have the opportunity to work with experts in photoreforming and explore photocatalytic H2 production using state-of-the-art equipment. Recent work has shown H2 evolution from waste using CdS as a photocatalyst. In this project I will apply the advanced CdS/CdSe materials I have developed for waste photoreforming. In addition, since CdS is toxic, I will apply my knowledge in low-dimensional nanomaterials to develop new photoreforming catalysts based on graphitic carbon nitride (gCN). gCN is a non-toxic, cheap and very stable 2D semiconductor that can be doped with individual metal ions to greatly enhance its catalytic activity and product selectivity.|A solar-driven low-cost process to generate H2 from waste holds great promise to provide renewable fuels while simultaneously addressing pollution, especially in developing countries with abundant sunlight.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Laser Driven Plasma Radiation Sources
descriptions: The interaction of high-power ultra-short lasers with materials offers exciting research which leads to some novel research. With the advent of multi-terawatt power lasers, exotic new plasmas with unique properties are now accessible, including strongly relativistic plasma. This intense laser interaction with matter offers new and unique opportunities in science, engineering, and medical application through the production of short, high flux pulses of energetic photons, neutrons, and positrons. Due to various advantages, laser-driven particle and radiation sources can replace much larger facilities such as synchrotron, cyclotrons. Laser-driven sources can also provide higher source brightness and shorter pulse duration than conventional particle facilities. The principal aim of this project is to investigate laser-driven X-ray sources. It has vast applications and could play a significant role in social development in terms of health and wellbeing. One of the major tasks of this project to produce bright, penetrating high-energy X-rays to make it applicable in X-ray radiography in medical science. These hard X-rays are able to provide 3-D views of human bone and capable of phase-contrast imaging of tumors. Ultrafast dynamics studies by laser-driven short X-ray pulse of any material is one of the objectives of this proposed project, which has the application on ultrafast imaging of biomedical samples. The proposal involves the development and implementation of new techniques on experiments using some of the highest power laser systems available at the University of Strathclyde (350 TW laser). This collaboration will have a positive impact on medical science via the exchange of innovative ideas.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Label-free detection of serotonin based on zinc oxide nanorod immunosensor
descriptions: I am applying to express my interest in an externship position for the 2020 Newton-Bhabha PhD Placement Programme. Currently, I am in second year of my doctoral study in the field of biosensor and expect to get a chance during coming summer. |My two years of research is at the interface of technology development towards real-time monitoring of monoamine neurotransmitter serotonin as a potent biomarker for early diagnosis of neurological disorders. The work builds up from developing a fundamental understanding of neurotransmitter events and creates diagnostics and therapeutics technologies to address global research challenges. |We first time designed rapidly grown zinc oxide nanorods field-effect transistor device based immunosensor for detection of serotonin molecule. We owe to develop portable immunosensor with a capacity to selectively target analytes through the antibody-antigen interaction strategy. Thereafter, the suitability of the fabricated sensor was used for the determination of various concentrations of serotonin ranging from a dynamic range of 1aM to 1 ÂµM in a buffer solution. The sensor sensitively measured different concentrations by impedance change within nanoseconds through the immunoreactions. Our designed sensor is applied to detect monoamine neurotransmitter serotonin in various real matrices to show its direct clinical applicability. Owing to the ease of miniaturization and label-free system we believe that the suggested device has the potential to be utilized for an implantable biosensor to detect neurotransmitter in the brain for diagnosis and treatment of neurological disorders. |My passion for technology development has provided me with new insights and unique skill set. The analytical skills I have honed in these two years of my research work will provide a strong foundation in research. I am specifically interested in this prestigious programme due to its unique approach to personal growth and tailored scientific solutions for each student. A commitment to support and train students and global opportunities offered through this international externship are invaluable. |If I get this opportunity I would be excited to join Dr. Mark Platt's laboratory. The laboratory has exceptional appeal for me because of its vital mission to foster portable sensors with a capacity to target analytes through aptamers by exciting methods which would be a part of my PhD context. As a biology researcher, I appreciate the comprehensive support of these analytical methodologies, particularly in this difficult situation of medical science towards disease diagnosis. I would like to focus on applying the research methodologies where aptamer functionalized particles, in combination with resistive pulse sensors are used to extract and quantify physiological analytes. So, I would relish this opportunity to leverage my past experiences for this worthy opportunity and learn from the experiences of my fellow team members at Loughborough University.|

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Hydrophilic and Amphiphilic Poly(vinylidene fluoride) Blend Ultrafiltration Membranes with Enhanced Antifouling Property
descriptions: Surface Engineering of Thin Film Composite Nanofiltration Membranes for Fluoride Removal:|Water is most essential for human activities and economic growth. Rapid industrial growth and urbanization, and some man-made and natural factors are responsible for increased water pollution. In my PhD work, I am working on preparation of Ultrafiltration membranes for the treatment of oily wastewater. Along with it I am involved in preparation of Nanofiltration (NF), Reverse osmosis (RO), and ion exchange membrane for removal of toxic contaminants and water desalination. Dr. Junjie Shen of University of Bath, working on fluoride removal from drinking water. He is also working on membrane based separation technology for fluoride removal. Fluorine is a natural element and it exists everywhere in all kind of soils. It is thirteenth most commonly available element in the earth's crust. It is found in ground water, sea water, and food. Fluoride exhibits both type of effect beneficial as well as detrimental on human health. According to the WHO's drinking water quality Guideline, the limit value for fluoride in drinking water is 1.5 mg/litre. In fluoride deficient area, fluoride salt is added in drinking water (around 1 mg/ L). Fluoride deficiency leads to tooth decay. In the places where the public drinking water and food contains excess amount of fluoride, skeletal fluorosis, discoloration, and bone fracture are the most observed adverse effects. An estimated amount of 27 million people in china are suffering from dental and skeletal fluorosis. Recently, membrane based separation processes get more attention for water desalination due to their lower cost and better performance property. Fluoride can easily remove by nanofiltration (NF) and reverse osmosis (RO) technology. The preparation if NF and Ro membranes involves two steps: (i) phase inversion and (ii) interfacial polymerization. It will give thin film composite NF/RO membrane based on choice of monomer for interfacial polymerization. The interfacial polymerization will form a polyamide thin film which is responsible for selective separation of solutes. We can prepare negatively charged NF and RO membranes by further modifications, which are capable of separating fluoride from drinking water. The negatively charged membranes can be developed by tuning the monomer concentration while preparing thin film composite (TFCs) membrane by interfacial polymerization. Piperazine and trimesoyl chloride (TMC) based negatively charged NF membranes will be effective for fluoride removal. NF/RO can also further modified by layer-by-layer (LBL) coating of oppositely charges polyelectrolytes on membrane surface which enhances the selectivity, rejection and antifouling behaviour of membranes. Modified NF and RO membranes can be highly effective for fluoride elimination and can provide quality drinking water to the society.|

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Fabrication of high performance thin films of Graphene and Graphene nanoribbons for transparent electronic and photovoltaic application|
descriptions: Transparent electrodes (TEs) play a crucial role in new generation technologies and devices such as solar cells, organic light emitting diodes (OLEDs), touch screens in laptops and mobile phone displays. These devices currently use indium tin oxide (ITO) or fluorine doped tin oxide (FTO) based electrodes. However, these electrodes are expensive and not flexible, therefore researchers all over the globe are searching for new materials to replace ITO. Transparent electrodes generally include transparent conductivity films, which are optically transparent and electrically conductive in thin layers. These have low sheet resistance. The main requirements of TE is its stability, it should work even under extreme environment conditions. Moreover, it should be compatible with almost any other material (base). We can say that it is a mechanically flexible with low material and processing costs.|Transparent conducting films (TCFs) are thin films of optically transparent and electrically conductive material. They are an important component in a number of electronic devices.  Transparent materials possess a wide band-gap. Solar cells requires a wider range of transparency beyond visible light to make efficient use of the full solar spectrum. ITO is the most widely used, alternatives include wider-spectrum transparent conductive oxides (TCOs). Films typically are made up of a layer of TCO, most commonly indium tin oxide (ITO), fluorine doped tin oxide (FTO). Organic films are being developed using carbon nanotubes (CNT) networks and Graphene, which can be fabricated to be highly transparent to visible and infrared light. ITO has the drawback of being expensive. Indium, the film's primary metal, is rare (6000 metric tons worldwide in 2006), and its price fluctuates due to market demand (over $800 per kg in 2006). ITO is not flexible; a small amount of strain as low as 2- 3% can initiate cracks in ITO film on flexible substrates, which reduces electrode conductivity and affects device performance. To reduce cost and increase performance, there is a clear need for a replacement transparent conductor for optoelectronic devices. This material should have high transparency and conductivity. Carbon-based nanomaterials such as Graphene, CNT are considered as suitable replacements to substitute traditional materials to manufacture TCE due to their remarkable characteristics, for example, high optical transmittance and outstanding electrical properties, good mechanical properties and low cost.|Purpose of Lab Visit:Their Lab produces high quality published scientific reports. I would be greatly thankful if I got opportunity to work with esteemed Faculty of UK institutes, with an opportunity to continue my Placement period as a part of the team under Dr Matthew Carnie. I believe my research activities and techniques will be suitable for your research field and also the experience in your group will be able to provide necessary opportunities for my research career.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Impact of Climate Variability on Pollen concentration, morphology & Pollinosis and application of Integrated Platform (GIS, Meteorological) for Public
descriptions: The variability in climatic conditions across the world due to accelerating anthropogenic activities induces prevalence of human diseases e.g. increased cardiovascular mortality and respiratory illnesses. Urban climate variability also plays an important role in deciding the fate of allergic diseases by changing allergen growth pattern. World Health Organization (WHO, 2017) estimated that globally 235 million people are suffering from asthma annually. Globally, pollens are considered as one the main triggers of respiratory allergies and skin infections in humans. ""Pollinosis"" due to pollens is the development of respiratory symptoms such as allergic rhinitis (hay fever), asthma, rhino-conjunctivitis as a result of pollen inhalation by the sensitive people. Pollens undergo physical as well as biochemical modification while travelling in lower troposphere as it is exposed to numerous atmospheric pollutants. Pollen distribution greatly depend on meteorological conditions, micro and macro topography of a particular area. Climatic factors, meteorological parameters and air pollutants are known to collectively interfere with the amount of pollen production, daily pollen concentration, length and time of pollen season, pollen distribution and allergen content, pollen fertility and pollen viability. |Keeping this in view, I started working for my Ph.D. thesis entitled ""Impact of Climate Variability on Pollen concentration, morphology & Pollinosis and application of Integrated Platform (GIS, Meteorological) for Public Health Risk Reduction"" under the supervision of Dr. Suman Mor (Panjab University, Chandigarh) and Dr. Ravindra Khaiwal (Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh) which aims to study the changing concentration of different pollen type and its relation with meteorological parameters. It also aims to study the health risks associated with Pollens by using standard questionnaire. |The proposed PhD placement work will allow to find the variability of the urban climate in response to the land cover type. As, increase in temperature, changes in landcover and shifts in the weather pattern have shown synergistic effect on dispersal and transportation of aeroallergens. The proposed placement will scientifically enhance the Ph.D. outcomes as it helps to identify the emission sources of pollens using back trajectory model along with WRF model. Moreover, this will help in building the relationship between emission area and its surroundings with airborne pollens concentration and to predict the dispersion of airborne pollen level in under-monitored areas.||The supervisors from the host institute are one of the global experts in the field of aerobiological research and this will provide me great opportunity to work with them to enhance my scientific knowledge and subsequently will help in building technical capacity of my parent institute. |

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: EXPEDITIOUS USE OF GOLD-CATALYSIS FOR THE SYNTHESES OF GLYCOCONJUGATES AND OLIGOSACCHARIDES
descriptions: We propose to work on the development of a new class of fluorescent mannoside-based nanoprobes for antimicrobial detection that is listed as one of the current biggest challenges in human health. Herein, we wish to amalgamate quantum dots and nanotechnology tools with that of glycan synthesis in order to develop fluorescent nanoprobes with an eventual understanding to detect microbial infections.||My PhD focuses on developing new methodologies for the synthesis of oligosaccharides and glycoconjugates which will be crucial for the success of the proposed research, while at the same time I will have the opportunity to get trained in complementary areas of research (e.g. nanotechnology, cell based assays and bio- imaging). I will be having ample scope to learn new skills which can be further useful for our lab and the whole department after I come back from Bristol. I will prepare a library of bacteria-specific mannoside glycans (IISER Pune) ready for nanoparticle conjugation (Bristol) using the strategies I have already developed during my PhD before I join Bristol to perform the nanoparticle conjugation and preliminary binding studies within the Galan group and collaborators in the Medical School (J. Spencer). Thus the fellowship offers an excellent and well-resourced framework within which to develop an exciting and productive collaborative program of research in Chemistry between the UK and India. In addition, I look forward to a greater collaboration between our department at IISER Pune and the School of Chemistry at University of Bristol and The Newton-Bhabha Fellowship will help in seeding this collaborative link and I am hopeful enough that this collaboration will be successful and results into a ERC grant and multiple publication in years to come.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Molecular and functional characterisation of small molecule inhibitors to evaluate anti-tumour activity in acute myeloid leukaemia
descriptions: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a type of blood cancer. The survival rate of patients is extremely poor which further decreases with age. The treatment option available comprises of highly toxic drugs. Despite the fact that these drugs are highly toxic, there are high chances of relapse and regardless of age most of the patients eventually die; nothing much has been done to improve treatment options for past thirty years. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop better therapeutic options for the treatment of AML. Recently, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved BCL2 specific inhibitor Venetoclax for elderly patients who are unfit for standard treatment with highly toxic drugs. Although early results of Venetoclax treatment in combination with hypomethylating agents are encouraging in AML but the emerging resistance to Venetoclax is a major concern in order to sustain long term remission. In view of this problem, we decided to identify a small molecule inhibitor which in combination with Venetoclax can overcome the resistance and further assist in killing the leukemic cells. The cyclin dependent kinases (CDKs) are becoming attractive targets to develop anti-cancer therapy. My project is in collaboration with Aurigene Discovery Technologies Limited, Bangalore. The Aurigene has provided a covalent, orally bioavailable and highly specific CDK7 inhibitor. This is the first orally bioavailable covalent inhibitor of CDK7. This novel drug (CDK7 inhibitor) has ability to specifically target the cancer cells and also it can overcome the problems associated with resistance to Venetoclax. In this project our aim is to identify effective combinatorial therapeutic options as an alternate of current standard of care. The host institute area of research is nicely overlapping with my PhD project. The Newton-Bhabha PhD placement, if awarded, will help my understanding of AML biology and identification of therapeutic targets using high throughput screening in which Professor Ken Mills (UK collaborator) laboratory has excellent proven track record. Through this placement, I would be exploring better, efficient and less toxic drug combination strategies to kill leukemia cells.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Simulation and Optimization of the Primary and Secondary Public Healthcare Delivery System
descriptions: My PhD research involves systematically analyzing the delivery of public primary and secondary healthcare delivery using computer simulation, with a focus on healthcare delivery in rural and semi-urban areas in India.|This involves developing simulation models of public primary and secondary healthcare delivery facilities using operational data collected during visits to these facilities. These simulation models are developed to establish the computational infrastructure required to analyse the operational performance (parameters such as average patient waiting time, time spent working for doctors and nurses, number of patients turned away, etc.) of these facilities. Such models can be used to estimate how operational performance of these facilities responds to changes in demand, operational patterns, etc. Further, the simulation models of these individual facilities will then be linked together to simulate the primary and secondary healthcare delivery network as a whole. We plan to develop this network simulation using metamodels of the individual facility simulation models. These metamodels are scaled down versions of the individual facility simulation models which still capture key operational performance aspects of the original models. They will enable implementing the network simulation in a computationally efficient manner.|The network simulation model will enable analysing the entire primary and secondary healthcare delivery network in a given district. This work could provide a way forward to other researchers in India and elsewhere regarding the development of healthcare delivery network simulations.    |In addition, we are also working on developing an optimization framework for optimal location of primary, secondary and tertiary healthcare delivery facilities in the Indian context. Under this formulation, we aim to minimize the cost of opening new healthcare facilities while ensuring that the demand for primary, secondary and tertiary care within an identified area is adequately covered. |At the University of Exeter, we plan to work closely with Prof. Navonil Mustafee, an expert on the application of simulation and operations research tools in healthcare in particular, on developing the public healthcare delivery network simulation as well as the optimal facility location problem. Working with Prof. Mustafee will help us improve the formulation and implementation of both types of models and evaluation of the results obtained. In addition, via interactions with the NHS in south-west England, we will explore how such methods of modelling and analysing public healthcare delivery can be applied in the UK and Western European contexts. Finally, we anticipate that this visit will help cement a collaborative relationship between IIT Delhi and the University of Exeter Business School, and in particular the Center for Simulation, Analytics and Modelling, with a focus on analysis of healthcare delivery systems in India and the UK.|

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Organic Spintronics: Spin-polarized current and spin-valve devices
descriptions: The electric charge, as well as the spin, is an integral part of all electrons. If an electron is depicted as a tiny planet, its spin will represent the direction of planet's rotation. Spin 'up' denotes clockwise rotation and spin 'down' stands for anticlockwise rotation. Using the up/down spin states instead of the 0 and 1 in the computer logic, one could transform the way of information processing.| By eradicating the charge movement, any such device would need less power and be less prone to overheating - removing some of the most major obstacles to further improving computer efficiency. So, inclusion of the spin to existing charge-based electronics (i.e. ""Spintronics"") is believed to add substantially more capability and also to give us faster, energy-efficient computers.| On this note, have you ever thought of that spintronics and organic chemistry (a sub-discipline of chemistry) have shared the same laboratory? Common answer is no. But these two disciplines have come closer to each other as researchers are trying to utilize organic molecules as transport medium of electron spin. Organic materials have the advantage of developing environmental friendly, low-cost, large area easy-processing electronics.
